lesson.title: Beyond the Screen: How Programs Read and Write Files
lesson.summary: File input and output, or file I/O, is how a Python program reads data from and writes data to files on disk, letting information outlive the program that created it, unlike the keyboard and screen which only handle data in the moment.
lesson.body:
You already know how a Python program talks to the outside world in the moment: `input()` pulls text in from the keyboard, and `print()` sends text out to the screen. The keyboard and the screen are input and output devices, the ones you use every single time a program runs. But everything that passes through them lives only in the computer's memory while the program is running. The instant the program ends, every variable, every string you typed, every value you printed, disappears. File input and output, usually just called file I/O, is how a program reads data from, and writes data to, files stored on disk instead, and a disk drive is another kind of I/O device, just a much more permanent one than a keyboard or a screen.

Reading a file means pulling its contents from disk into your program as data you can work with, almost always as strings of text. Writing a file means pushing strings from your program out to a file that will still be sitting on the disk after the program has finished and the computer has been turned off and back on again. This is the difference between memory and storage: memory is fast but temporary, storage is slower but persistent. Nearly every real program relies on this persistence somewhere: a game saves your progress, a text editor saves your document, a web browser logs your history, a script writes out a report other people will open later.

Getting from "my program has some data" to "that data is sitting in a file on disk" always follows the same basic shape: open a connection to the file, read from it or write to it, then close that connection when you are done. Python's built in `open()` function is the gateway for all of this, and later chapters in this sequence will dig into exactly how it works, what modes it accepts, and the safer ways to make sure a file gets closed. For now, here is the whole round trip in miniature, writing a short greeting to a file and then reading it back.

```python
file = open("greeting.txt", "w")
file.write("Hello, file!")
file.close()

file = open("greeting.txt", "r")
contents = file.read()
file.close()

print(contents)
```

The first `open()` call, using mode `"w"`, creates `greeting.txt` (or empties it out if it already existed) and hands back a file object that `write()` sends text through. Calling `close()` finishes that connection. The second `open()` call, using mode `"r"`, opens the same file for reading, and `read()` pulls its entire contents back as one string, which gets stored in `contents`. Printing `contents` shows exactly what was written:

```python
Hello, file!
```

Notice that nothing about `contents` reveals it came from a file rather than, say, being typed in directly. That is the whole point: once the data is read in, it behaves like any other Python string, ready to be searched, split, or transformed using everything you already know about strings and the rest of the Python language. The next few chapters build out exactly how `open()`, reading, and writing really work, mode by mode and method by method.
